senses: The state of being, or behavior and thought, of heathens.
ety: From heathen + -ism, coined in the 17th century in place of the then-obsolete heathendom. First attested in Francis Bacon's Of the advancement of learning (1605), II. xiv. §9: "The heresy of the Anthropomorphites … and the opinion of Epicurus, answerable to the same in heathenism, who supposed the gods to be in human shape" (OED).

senses: Someone (usually a soldier) equipped with a crossbow.
examples: Why did Richard I die at the hands of a crossbowman, clutching a frying pan, on the outskirts of Limoges?

senses: One who colours; an artist with a talent for colouring
A hairdresser who is a specialist in colouring and tinting hair.
Anything that differentiates, or causes differentiation (in any sense); a distinguishing feature.
To make joyful or proud.
To lift up; raise; elevate.
ety: From Middle English elat, elate, from Latin ēlātus (“exalted, lofty”), perfect passive participle of efferō (“bring forth or out; raise; exalt”), see -ate (verb-forming suffix).

senses: Not printable; obscene, or unable to be displayed textually.
examples: Once a neighbor complained that a Gilbreth had called the neighbor's boy a son of an unprintable word.

senses: Wooded; bearing timber; forested.
Made from timber, especially large or coarsely finished timber.
examples: His steps were imperceptibly led almost in a circle; nor did he observe that he was on the verge of a tract of land heavily timbered, but not with pine-trees.
The booking hall is lofty and of peculiar design, the roof being carried on timbered beams set in pairs rising from carved corbels.

senses: A man who is engaged in an erotic relationship with an adolescent boy; a practitioner of pederasty.
ety: Borrowed from French pédéraste, from Ancient Greek παιδεραστής (paiderastḗs, “lover of boys”), from παῖς (paîs, “boy”) and ἐραστής (erastḗs, “lover”).

senses: Someone or something that steers.
A person hired by a gambling establishment to locate potential customers and bring them in.
A person who makes knots.
A machine or device that makes knots.
A screen used to remove “knots” or impurities from wood pulp in the process of making paper.
A new immigrant (usually to the UK).
A freshwater crocodile (Crocodylus johnstoni)
ety: From fresh + -ie. In the sense of an immigrant, shortened from fresh off the boat.

senses: surrounding a tooth
ety: From Ancient Greek περί (perí, “around”) + ὀδούς (odoús, “a tooth”).

senses: A pale greyish white colour, tinted with blue.
examples: Pearly is that silky and often coloured lustre which renders of such value
When (the scales are) more developed and thickened, the color (pearly) is deepened, shading

senses: The Soviet machinery of state bureaucratic administration, or a similar communistic structure.
ety: Borrowed from Russian аппара́т (apparát, “apparatus, apparat”). Doublet of apparatus.

senses: A motor vehicle for transporting horses.
A container for transporting horses in, whether by road, rail, or sea.
Deeply rooted; persistent.
examples: Rickie would not push himself. It was his besetting sin.
I did not then know the besetting sin of woman, the passion to discuss her private affairs with anyone who is willing to listen.

senses: A food product made of cornmeal.
ety: Borrowed from Swahili posho, itself from English portion.

senses: The study of symbolic representation, especially of the origin and meaning of Scripture types.
The systematic classification of the types of something according to their common characteristics.
The result of the classification of things according to their characteristics.
The doctrine of Scripture types or figures.
A magical or mysterious force; hypnotic power; energy.
examples: I don't say she would have done anything, if it had come to the point; but the fluence was on, and she got me hot.

senses: A person or thing detained; a detainee.
ety: From late Middle English detenue, from Old French detenue, feminine singular past participle of detenir (“to detain”). See detain.

senses: The alkali produced from the plant, an impure carbonate of soda, used for making soap, glass, etc., and for bleaching.
Impure soda obtained from the ashes of any seashore plant, or kelp.
examples: Good barilla usually contains, according to Dr. Ure's analysis, 20 per cent. of real alkali, associated with muriates and sulphates, chiefly of soda, some lime, and alumina, with very little sulphur.

senses: A form of printing on paper from a glass sheet to which oil paint has been applied; monotype.
A kind of Italian lemon-flavoured liqueur.
A glass of this drink.
ety: Borrowed from Italian limoncello, a diminutive of limone (“lemon”).

senses: Most winning; most attractive.
A sap-sucking insect pest of the superfamily Aphidoidea; an aphidian.
ety: From New Latin aphis (plural aphides), coined by Swedish botanist Carolus Linnaeus in 1758. His inspiration for the name remains unclear; OED suggests it might stem from a misreading of Ancient Greek κορις (koris, “bug”) (see diagram), in which case the nominative -ις (-is) suffix was reanalyzed as -ις, -ιδος (-is, -idos); while AHD suggests a connection to Ancient Greek ἀφειδής (apheidḗs, “unsparing, lavishly borrowed”) in reference to the insects' voracity or rapid rate of production, from ἀ- (a-, “not”) + φείδομαι (pheídomai, “to spare, be thrifty, be merciful”), ultimately from Proto-Indo-

senses: An embryonic organism, grown in vitro from a few cells
To render into dust or powder.
To completely destroy, especially by crushing to fragments or a powder.
To defeat soundly, thrash.
To become reduced to powder; to fall to dust.
ety: From Middle English pulverizen, from Latin pulverizō, pulverizāre, from pulvis (“powder”). Compare French pulvériser. By surface analysis, pulver (“powder”) + -ise.

senses: A pot for cooking or serving beans.
examples: Everywhere in the colonies potbakers' workshops supplied local people with plain red-clay mugs and beanpots, jugs and milkpans for kitchen and dairy.
There were three miniature beanpots of brown pottery filled with steaming baked beans topped with slices of crisp salt pork.

senses: a viceroy or vicereine
A member of a particular sect, school of thought or practice, party, or profession; a sectarian.
A Protestant dissenter or nonconformist.
ety: Either from the French sectaire or directly from its etymon, the Medieval Latin sectārius, from secta (“sect”). Cognates include the Italian settario and the Portuguese and Spanish sectario.
examples: Be it as it may: within the Land of Penn / The sectary yielded to the citizen, / And peaceful dwelt the many-creeded men.

It is this spirit which inspires sectaries to deprecate the public schools and, if they cannot divert part of the tax support, then to foist upon this free system the shadow of their own beclouded vision.

senses: Synonym of dupatta – a long scarf worn by South Asian women.
ety: Borrowed from Punjabi چُنّی (cunnī) / Punjabi ਚੁੰਨੀ (cunnī).
examples: Her head was covered with a green and yellow bandhani chunni which was tucked into the cleavage of her blouse.
She no longer wears the scarf, called a chunni, while she works.

senses: A phalanstery.
ety: From Middle English phalange, from Middle French phalange, from Old French phalange, from Latin phalanx (accusative phalangem), from Ancient Greek φάλαγξ (phálanx). Doublet of phalanx, planch, plancha, planche, and plank.

senses: A Russian noble knight who rode a horse.
A screenshot.
A screensaver.
Someone who spends a lot of time in front of a (television or computer) screen.
examples: Screenies: these boys spent very large amounts of time in front of a screen of some sort — 10 per cent of boys spend over seven hours every day in front of a screen — but had low levels of physical activity and sleep.
The study found three clusters of boys: 'sporties', 'screenies' and 'autonomes' (the last group spending a lot of time in self-starting pursuits, either by themselves or with peers).

senses: A dark brownish-red colour.
The blood of an ox.
examples: Ryckeboer’s map shows the different complementisers used in the sentence Ik moet ossebloed drinken om te verkloeken lit. I must oxblood drink for to recover ‘I have to drink oxblood to recover.’
Mr. Mac informed me that it was treated with oxblood and bee’s wax.
The Greeks said that after the defeat Midas committed suicide by drinking oxblood (Strabo 1, 3, 21).

senses: Not capable of being said.
examples: Nonetheless, in some unsayable way, value sentences are about values and reflect the structure of values.
The unsaid drives us to “speak;” but, in some ways, there are limitations on what we can say, because some part always remains unsaid — we must always attempt to say the unsayable.

senses: A healthful, stimulating kind and level of stress.
ety: From eu- + stress, coined by contrast with distress, as if interpreting the latter as dys- + stress.

senses: The fatty components of milk and other dairy products.
A reptile, Sphenodon punctatus, native to New Zealand, that resembles a lizard and is the only surviving specimen of the order Rhynchocephalia.
Between hemispheres, especially between the two hemispheres of the brain.
